div.p: We used maximum likelihood approach to identify the best-fitting model of population dynamics described with these three sub-models in our study. First, we modeled detection probability as a function of observation-level covariates (stream noise, time of survey, day of year of the survey, wind speed, weather, and a quadratic term for the day of year of the survey). Then, we modeled the initial abundance as a function of vegPC1, vegPC2, elevation, and the quadratic term of elevation. Therefore, if trends in species' populations are predictable as a function of the interaction between either of these vegetation indices (vegPC1, vegPC2) and microclimate (tempPC1) this would constitute support for the insurance hypothesis. We used likelihood ratio tests between the null model (intercept-only trend sub-model and full detection and initial abundance sub model) and the hypothesis model for each species to test our hypotheses. We used significance level of 0.1 as a criterion for statistical support, to reduce the potential risk of type 2 error, when analyzing complex process that involves interaction effects in a weakly controlled field setting.

Before testing our hypotheses, we first selected the appropriate mixing statistical distribution for abundance (between Poisson versus Zero-inflated Poisson distributions) using Akaike's Information Criteria (AIC). Then we checked for the model identifiability, by comparing the negative log-likelihood as the K increases toward 400. K is a nuisance parameter that sets the maximum boundary for the abundance space, to make fitting process efficient. To reduce computation time and ensure that the fitted models were within the boundary of parameter space, we chose the lowest value of K that showed a stabilized minimum negative log-likelihood (Ké ry 2018, Ké ry and Royle 2020). To choose the distribution for abundance and K values, we set covariates for initial abundance and detection probability models as above, but we used an intercept-only model for the trend sub-model. Among the 23 selected species, we were able to identify 20 species' models for which log-likelihood and initial abundance estimates converged as K increased to 400 (Appendix Figure 3.2, 3.3).

div.head: Results
div.p: Over the 8-year study period, six of twenty species declined, while nine species increased, with five species exhibiting little statistical support for a trend (2011-2018;Figure 3.4). Among all species examined, eight species showed strong statistical support for either the microclimate buffering hypothesis or the insurance hypothesis (likelihood ratio test p < 0.1; Table 3.1, species shown in Figure 3.5).

Microclimate had a negative effect on population trends of these eight species indicating that local (point level) abundance decreased at greater rates in warmer areas than in cooler areas (Figure 3.5AB). This relationship supports the microclimate buffering hypothesis, and is consistent with the idea that cooler microclimates created by old-growth vegetation and topography can provide refugia for organisms, over the 8 years that were sampled. Among these 8 species, Wilson's Warbler, Golden-crowned Kinglet, Hermit

Warbler and Chestnut-backed Chickadees declined, suggesting that average conditions across the watershed were associated with declining population trends. Three other species, Pacific Wren, Pacificslope Flycatcher, and Swainson's Thrush increased, even though their trends were negatively related to warmer microclimates.

We did not find strong support for the insurance hypothesis; statistical interactions between vegetation (vegPC1 and vegPC2) and microclimate were generally not well supported. However, for a few species, we found weak evidence that vegPC2 moderates the effect of microclimate on population trends; 90% confidence intervals for the interactions terms between vegPC2 and microclimate only narrowly bounded zero (Fig. 5A &B). For Wilson's Warbler and Red Crossbills, higher compositional diversity (lower vegPC2) reduced the negative effect of warmer microclimate on the population trend (i.e., the interaction between vegPC2 and microclimate was negative; Figure 3.5). However, for Golden-crowned Kinglet and Pacific Wren, greater amount of deciduous tree species, low coniferous tree diversity and high canopy cover reduced negative effects of warmer microclimate on their trends (i.e. the interaction between vegPC2 and microclimate was positive; Figure 3.5).
Two species showed evidence for additive main effect of vegetation (either vegPC1 or vegPC2).
Swainson's Thrush had more positive trends in areas with higher structural complexity (higher vegPC1).

With the confidence interval including zero, Wilson's Warbler had more positive trends in areas with higher canopy heterogeneity and plant diversity, being negatively related to the vegPC2 index (higher diversity in plants and canopy height when it is negative; Figure 3.5).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: We used fine-resolution, below-canopy temperature loggers to test whether long-term bird population trends are affected by microclimate, and whether vegetation structure and composition can mediate microclimate effects. Indeed, some cooler microclimates potentially provided by old-growth structure and topography seem to be advantageous for some species. In addition, old-growth, and diverse second-growth to have greater complexity could provide critical microclimatic refugia across the region, which could mitigate declines in sub-populations within a larger metapopulation context (Hanski 1998, Hannah et al. 2014, Morelli et al. 2020).

Although we did not test the mechanisms for negative impacts of warming on bird population trends, previous research on avian physiology and ecology suggests potential mechanisms. First, thermal stress from warming temperatures increases metabolic rates; it becomes energetically costly for birds to thermoregulate via physiological and behavioral modifications (Gerson et al. 2019, Conradie et al. 2019, McKechnie and Wolf 2019, van de Ven et al. 2020). Such costs can be especially detrimental for breeding birds that need to meet high energetic requirements of reproduction. All four declining species are small passerine species and may have high-energy requirements during breeding season (Cucco andMalacarne 1997, Nagy andHolmes 2005). Energy expenditure may amplify when thermal optima are exceeded during the mid-breeding season (Wolf and Walsberg 1996, Grémillet et al. 2012, O'Connor et al. 2021).

A second potential mechanism affecting trends in bird populations is limitation in food availability during an energetically demanding period. Warmer microclimates would advance leaf-out and arthropod emergence, well before timing of the peak requirements during the nesting season (matchmismatch ;Cushing 1990). This may be most detrimental for long-distance migrants like Hermit Warblers that seem to have limited phenotypic plasticity for spring arrival dates (Mayor et al. 2017b, Robinson et al. 2019), and in some cases, cause drastic declines in breeding population of a migratory bird species (Both et al. 2006(Both et al. , 2010)). This mechanism can also apply to sedentary species, but the mismatch may be less drastic (Burgess et al. 2018). Nonetheless, fitness loss and a reduced probability of double brooding may result from an increasing mismatch between resource availability and resource needs for some species (Reed et al. 2013). These potential phenological mismatches will vary spatially, leading to locations on a landscape where both availability of resources and suitable microclimates may increase individual fitness, but reduce it in others (Burgess et al. 2018, Kwon et al. 2019, Shutt et al. 2019, Jeong et al. 2020). Thus, how these mismatches are manifested over subpopulations or entire geographic ranges is not clear.

We hypothesized that the potential negative effect of temperatures on food availability can be alleviated by compositional and structural diversity that provide protracted resource availability and prey redundancy (insurance hypothesis; Figure 3.1B). There was weak evidence of insurance provided by structural and compositional diversity in four species of birds that are negatively affected by warmer microclimate in our study (Figure 3.5B). In these species, increases or decreases in vegPC2 mediated the strength of negative microclimate effect on trends, although we only had weak statistical support for these interaction effects (Figure 3.5A). Notably, a decrease in vegPC2, which is strongly related to tree species richness, understory woody plant richness and cover, DBH diversity and canopy cover diversity and amount of snag and decaying wood (Figure 3.2), reduced negative effects of a warming microclimate for Potential insurance effects on Pacific Wren and Golden-crowned Kinglet are less clear because a higher vegPC2 was associated with reducing the negative effects of warmer microclimates. Higher vegPC2 estimates are related to low tree and understory woody plant species diversity, low canopy cover diversity, low DBH diversity, but it is positively related to canopy cover and proportion of deciduous trees (Figure 3.3). Because woody plant species richness at the HJA is mainly driven by understory woody plant diversity and coniferous tree species diversity, deciduous tree species such as Bigleaf Maple or Red Alder had a minor effect on tree species richness in closed-canopy forests. However, closedcanopy forests with deciduous trees were more common in the valley bottoms, where Pacific Wrens occur more frequently (Toews and Irwin 2020). Pacific Wrens feed on invertebrates in soil layers and undercanopy vegetation, which may be more available with high moisture levels in valley bottoms, where these deciduous trees can grow (Ellis 2020, Williamson et al. 2021). Golden-crowned Kinglets, on the contrary, are foliage-gleaning species that are associated with continuous conifer canopy cover; we speculate that a more continuous, uniform canopy and high amounts of deciduous trees (i.e., higher vegPC2) may provide resources that can assist in mediating negative effects of warmer microclimate, but the explanation remains unknown.

Redundancy in producers and (compositional diversity/richness of plants) that can be delivered to secondary consumers (birds) may be providing an insurance effect for these bird populations under a warming climate. Previous studies have shown that such interactions occur in coffee agroecosystems, where shade coffee farms with more floristic diversity received greater predation pressure on artificial arthropod prey items from wild birds (Valone and Barber 2008), or increased tree diversity is related to within-season stability in bird community characteristics (May-Uc et al. 2020). The ability of vegetation to mediate microclimate effects on population trends was not detected for other species in our study. This may be due to lack of such strong interaction effects, because: 1) Microclimate effects were overwhelmingly strong and species are specialized to certain resources that cannot be subsidized by other 'redundant' resources provided by compositional and structural diversity of the forest; 2) Our sampling gradient may lack not cover the range of diversity across the microclimatic gradient that is needed to detect an interaction effect (we may lack fully balanced design due to our topography and vegetation distribution); 3) unexplained non-breeding season drivers, both for migratory and sedentary species play greater role than breeding season microclimate; or 4) our dimension-reduced PCA indices did not represent the key dimension of redundancy in resource diversity. While our PCA indices summarize the forest vegetation in two dimensions, both axes of first and second principal components (vegPC1 vegPC2) are related to compositional and structural diversity of forest vegetation, and it may not necessarily pinpoint key resource diversity that may mediate microclimate effects. In a meta-analysis of 466 studies across various systems, insurance effects were stronger from in vitro experiments that controlled biodiversity more strictly, compared to experiments conducted in field plots (Balvanera et al. 2006). Complexity and landscape-level heterogeneity in our study system is not comparable to those of in vitro experiments but also of those controlled field plot experiments. Thus, it is not surprising to have low statistical power in our tests for interaction effects. However, considering the existing heterogeneity and complex ecological interactions in the forested landscape, our study has real-world implications for forest bird and ecosystem conservation (Balvanera et al. 2006).

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Our findings suggest that old-growth forest characteristics can provide climate refugia for some species over the short term at least. In a recent study, Rosenberg et al. (2019) reported that western forest birds have declined by 29.5% since from 1970 to 2018. Although the mechanisms of these mass declines in western forests are still unclear, recent research suggests that old-growth forest associated species are in declinedespite current conservation policy measures (Phalan et al. 2019). In addition, climate-change driven spring and summer warming in the Pacific Northwest would deteriorate breeding habitat of forest birds in the region (Betts et al. 2018, Northrup et al. 2019).

It is an open question whether or not this buffering effect can be maintained as regional temperatures continue to rise, and changes to forest show that if a species is associated with cooler temperatures, rate of change in abundance will be lower in the warmer microclimate, and vice versa. div.head: Introduction
div.p: Understanding migratory behavior and population connectivity throughout the full annual cycle is essential for the conservation of migratory birds (Webster et al. 2002, Newton 2008, Kirby et al. 2008b, Faaborg et al. 2010b, Marra et al. 2015). Environmental conditions at each stage of the annual cycle can influence individual behavior and fitness, altering species' distributions and population trends (Rushing et al. 2017). For example, degradation of habitat and climate conditions on wintering grounds could increase mortality during this non-breeding period, and could influence spring phenology of migration and breeding, followed by subsequent changes in reproductive success (Sillett and Holmes 2002, Newton 2006, Both et al. 2010). Under the current rate of climate change, knowing these population linkages is essential for conservation of climate-sensitive migratory species under the current rate of climate change and habitat loss (Parmesan 2006, Rushing et al. 2016a, Abatzoglou and Williams 2016, Berner et al. 2017, Phalan et al. 2019, Furnas 2020).

The term 'migratory connectivity' describes the linkage between migratory populations at breeding and wintering grounds. When connectivity is strong, populations from the breeding grounds do not mix with each other on the wintering grounds; if individuals from different breeding grounds intermix in the wintering grounds, the migratory connectivity is diffuse (Webster et al. 2002, Cohen et al. 2018, Somveille et al. 2021). Spatial patterns of migratory connectivity are typically grouped into three categories: in telescopic migration birds from all latitudes gather at the same location (Alerstam andHedenström 1998, Newton 2008). In chain migration, northern breeding populations migrate to northern parts of the nonbreeding range and southern populations migrate farther south. Alternatively, "leap-frog migration" occurs when northern breeding populations migrate to the furthest portions of the nonbreeding range, leaping over southern breeding populations that winter in northern portions of the nonbreeding range (Salomonsen 1955, Alerstam and Hedenström 1998, Newton 2008, Somveille et al. 2021).

Migration pattern needs to be understood together with migration phenology of birds. For many migratory birds, the migration phenology closely tracks the spatial distribution of food availability (Renfrew et al. 2013, La Sorte et al. 2016, Visser and Gienapp 2019b, Helm et al. 2019). Seasonal climatic cycles are the most common drivers of the timing of peak resource availability (Kharouba et al. 2018, Renner andZohner 2018), and many small passerine species rely on pulses of food availability for breeding and migration (Both et al. 2010, Visser et al. 2012, Burgess et al. 2018). To reach breeding and non-breeding destinations at the time when the conditions are optimal for fitness, many migratory bird species use different migration routes and move at differing rates during spring versus fall migration (Newton 2008, Mckinnon et al. 2013, Morin et al. 2020). Among many factors, wind conditions (Klaassen et al. 2010, Limiñana et al. 2013), resource availability for refueling (Alerstam 2001, Rousseau et al. 2020) or molting (Holmgren andHedenström 1995, Siegel et al. 2016), and sexual selection (Kokko 1999) are often suggested as drivers of differential migration speed and route in spring and fall. However, it remains unclear which drivers are most important, or how these major drivers are related to differences in migratory routes and rates between spring and fall migration.

Hermit Warblers breed only in montane coniferous forests of the Pacific Northwest region of the United States, where they are a common warbler species (Sauer et al. 2017, Betts et al. 2018, Furnas 2020).

As one of the more abundant avian secondary consumers in the canopy food web, the species can potentially play an important role in providing ecological functions and services in these forests, as other songbird communities do in early-seral forests (Campbell et al. 1983, Harris et al. 2020). The total population of Hermit Warblers seems to have declined in recent years (1993-2019;Sauer et al. 2020). Rushing et al. (2016b) demonstrated that populations of Hermit Warblers across their breeding range have distinct groups that share similar demographic parameters, and the most recent North American Breeding Bird Survey data suggest that rates of decline vary among regions, with birds in the Sierra Nevada and Washington declining most rapidly during the past two decades (Sauer et al. 2020). Hermit Warblers are considered a species of concern in the Sierra Nevada Bird Conservation Region by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2021). Even with the their ecological importance and concerning future,
we know little about their migration ecology that is essential for understanding their population processes (Pearson 2020).

Climate change and habitat loss may partly explain variability in Hermit Warbler population trends throughout the breeding range (Betts et al. 2018, Phalan et al. 2019, Northrup et al. 2019). Breeding habitat loss from increased fire frequency, intensive forest management, and climate change is predicted across their breeding range in the future (Bell et al. 2014, Hicke et al. 2016, Abatzoglou and Williams 2016, Berner et al. 2017, Stevens-Rumann and Morgan 2019). Yet, the effects of wintering ground climate and land-use change remain uncertain. We know little about how Hermit Warbler breeding populations are dispersed in the overwintering range, so it is challenging to associate changes in wintering ground climate or habitat to particular breeding ground populations. Hermit Warbler breeding and wintering grounds both extend across a broad latitudinal gradient (Figure 4.1), and many aspects of the species' migratory ecology, including connectivity, spatial pattern, phenology, behavior and routes, are poorly known.

Here, we reveal the migration movements of Hermit Warblers throughout the annual cycle, using light-level archival tags (geolocators). We document annual migration routes, timing, and wintering locations of Hermit Warblers from six locations across their breeding grounds, covering more than 900 kilometers north-south in the western United States. More specifically, we analyze: 1) migratory connectivity and spatial patterns of migrating Hermit Warblers, 2) the timing of migration related to breeding and wintering ground location, 3) the migration routes of Hermit Warblers during spring and fall, and 4) duration of migration and distribution of daily migration rates during the fall and spring migration.

div.head: Study area
div.p: We selected seven study sites across the Hermit Warbler's breeding range, from Washington to California (Figure 4.1). All of our study sites were montane coniferous forest, but tree species composition of stands varied among sites, from pure Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii) or Western White Fir (Abies concolor) stands in plantation forests in Oregon and Washington, to Sierra mixedconifer forests in California and old-growth Douglas Fir-Western Hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla) stands in Oregon and Washington (Table 4.1). Study sites varied in elevation from 100 -2200 m. We selected specific capture locations within each study site based on accessibility and detections of Hermit Warbler during previous visits. We attempted to sample birds from forests across a broad range of tree species diversity, canopy height, and tree size heterogeneity. We recorded the coordinates of capture locations with handheld GPS units (Garmin GPS62, Garmin, USA) with a 3-to 4-meter error range.

div.head: Geolocator deployment and retrieval
div.p: To track locations of birds across the annual cycle, we attached 177 geolocators to adult (second year and after-second year) male Hermit Warblers. In 2018, birds were tagged only at H.J. Andrews

Experimental Forest and MacDonald Forest (N=61), and in 2019, birds were tagged across all seven sites (N=116, Figure 4.1, Table 4.1). We captured birds with mist nets, facilitated by plastic decoys and audio lures. Geolocators (Model: ML6340, Lotek Wireless Inc., UK) were deployed on birds using a modified leg-loop harness made with elastic jewelry cord (Rappole andTipton 1991, Streby et al. 2015).

Geolocators were 0.38-0.43 g, and were less than 5% of the body mass of the birds. All birds with geolocators were marked with unique combinations of two or three color bands, and a U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service metal band with unique numbers. A year later, we attempted to recapture or re-sight each bird by revisiting initial capture locations and surroundings within 250 m. We recaptured birds using the same methods that we used for initial captures, but unlike during initial capture efforts, multiple nets or revisits were often necessary. Before attaching and after detaching geolocators from each bird, we recorded basic morphometrics (i.e., wing, tarsus, skull length and body mass) using a wing ruler, calipers, and an electronic scale.

With this buffered range map, we created a spatial mask that allows locations over water and outside the range boundary, but at one tenth the likelihood of locations within the range boundary (Cooper et al. 2017). Then, we calibrated the timing of twilight from both the breeding and wintering periods. We used the known breeding territory locations (location of capture as true location) of each tagged bird during the breeding season (tag deployment to July 2nd in the first year and May 1st to the tag retrieval date in the second year) for calibrating geolocator location estimates on the breeding range. This is a conservative window of the stationary period at breeding sites when we caught and recaptured Hermit Warblers.

Hermit Warblers use different light environments between the breeding season and non-breeding periods; they breed in dense, closed-canopy conifer stands and winter in relatively open montane mixed conifer-broadleaf forests (Pearson 2020). Thus, we calibrated the non-breeding season twilight timings using the Hill-Ekstrom method, for October 15 to March 15. This approach includes periods influenced by equinoxes, and when the birds are thought to be stationary based on the exploratory location estimates.

We limited movement rates to fall within the speed of migration for similar songbirds (i.e., Kirtland's Warbler Setophaga kirtlandii; Ewert et al. 2012) by using a speed distribution (km/h; gamma distribution with shape =2.3, rate =0.5). We first ran the modified gamma model with 1000 iterations and tuned the model with six chains of each with 1000 iterations. We ran the final model with 3000 MCMC samples, and median location estimates (longitude and latitudes) were obtained for each twilight event. With these final MCMC samples, we proceeded with a post-hoc summary and analyses of locations.
Identification of breeding and winter range, and the timing of arrivals and departures.

We used each individual bird's distribution of locations throughout their full annual tracks to create spatial thresholds for identifying breeding and wintering periods. First, we set a spatial threshold for wintering and breeding periods for each bird based on its migratory behavior. We defined a spatial threshold for the breeding range, as 0.5 degrees latitude and longitude from the location of recapture, and the threshold for winter range at each individual's easternmost 25th percentile longitude of year-round locations. We only used longitude for setting this threshold because latitude was not useful during fall and spring equinoxes, when birds often left or arrived at the wintering locations. After defining spatial boundaries for each individual's breeding and wintering ranges, we used the date of the bird's first passage through the boundary without returning to identify winter and breeding periods. For defining wintering locations, we used the median of the MCMC samples of latitude and longitude when each bird entered the wintering range as point estimate of their winter location (Figure 4.2).

div.head: Migratory connectivity and migration pattern
div.p: We used a Mantel correlation to assess migratory connectivity of birds from Gifford Pinchot National Forest, H.J. Andrews Experimental Forest and Yosemite National Park (the locations with data from more than two returning birds). The Mantel test calculates the correlation between distances among birds on the breeding grounds and distances among birds on the wintering grounds (Ambrosini et al. 2009, Somveille et al. 2021). Higher Mantel correlation coefficients (rM; closer to 1) indicate strong migratory connectivity (i.e., birds from the same breeding location are clustered together on the wintering grounds). Alternatively, a Mantel correlation coefficient near zero indicates a lack of such clustering. We calculated the statistical significance of the Mantel correlation using 10 6 permutations. Mantel correlation was calculated with function "mantel" in the R package "vegan", with distance between points measured on the earth's surface (WGS84 ellipsoid), using the package "geosphere".

We used Bayesian linear mixed effect models to describe relationships between breeding and winter locations. We set breeding site as a random effect variable, to allow the intercept of each relationship to vary by site and to account for potential similarity among individuals within sites. We standardized location variables, so that regression slopes for each model would be comparable. div.head: Migratory phenology and its relationships with locations and subsequent migration phenology
div.p: We aimed to assess if breeding or wintering locations of birds are related to the arrival and departure timing to those locations. This is based on the potential spatial gradient in phenology of producers and arthropod prey that birds rely on for breeding and during wintering periods. For example, birds breeding at more northern breeding grounds may depart later from the wintering grounds, and arrive later to the breeding grounds.

div.head: Migration routes and rates between spring and fall migration
div.p: We described migration routes of birds using the path connecting median locations between the day of departure from the breeding range to the day of arrival at the winter range (fall migration) and the day of departure from the winter range to the day of arrival at the breeding range (spring migration) in the following year. Because the latitudinal estimates during an equinox are unreliable (Lisovski et al. 2020),

we avoided interpreting the path during 15 days before and after the fall and spring equinox. We calculated daily migration rates (km/day) during fall and spring migration for every 5-day interval after departure from the breeding or winter range. We compared the duration of migration (number of days) for fall and spring migration using a paired t-test for each individual bird. We used the difference between fall and spring migration duration for each bird as a response variable, with "t.test" function in base R program. We used program R version 4.0.5. for all analysis and data preparation in this study.

div.head: Recapture rates and comparison between control birds and tagged birds
div.p: We recaptured 11 and 14 birds with geolocators in 2019 and 2020, respectively. In 2020, we recaptured at least one tagged bird from six study sites but failed to retrieve any birds with geolocators the Klamath Lake site (Table 4.1). Three tags from 2019 malfunctioned and did not record locations from the full annual cycle, and one tag had too many shading events to provide reliable information; we excluded those individuals from the analyses. In addition to the recaptured birds, we observed and identified ten individual birds with unique color band combinations but were unable to recapture them (five birds in each year), making total return rates 17% in 2019-2020 and 26% in 2018-2019

div.head: Migratory phenology and its relationships with locations and subsequent migration phenology
div.p: In fall, birds departed breeding grounds from late June to late July (mean = July 7, s.d. = 11.9), arriving at their winter location in late September to early October (mean = October 3, s.d. = 16.5). In spring, they left wintering grounds in late March to early April (mean = March 29, s.d. = 9.6) and arrived at breeding grounds in early May (mean = May 9, s.d. = 6.4). Departure dates from breeding grounds in fall were not related to wintering or breeding locations. However, birds wintering farther south generally arrived at wintering grounds later than birds wintering farther north (slope = -0.459, 90% CI = -0.904 --0.034), and birds wintering farther west departed wintering grounds later than birds wintering farther east (slope = -0.522, 90% CI = -0.845 --0.198). There was weak statistical evidence for the relationship between winter site departure dates and breeding ground locations, and between the breeding site arrival dates and breeding latitude. This pattern may be due to the leveraging influence of the three birds from Yosemite that wintered in the most eastern and southern locations and started migration from the wintering grounds earlier than other birds (Appendix Table 4.1, Table 4.2), which may indicate a need for further investigation of migration patterns for the southern populations. For each subsequent migration phenology date, birds arriving earlier at the breeding sites also departed their wintering site earlier than others, indicating a more constrained time-budget for spring migration (slope = 0.497, 90% CI = 0.124 -0.869), but not between breeding site departure and winter site arrival, and between winter site arrival and winter site departure dates (Table 4.2).

div.head: Migratory connectivity and pattern
div.p: Although limited by small sample sizes at each study location, we did not find evidence for strong migratory connectivity, indicating minimal segregation in wintering grounds by breeding locations.

Birds tagged at H.J. Andrews, where we had the greatest sample size, were distributed widely across Mexico during the winter period, also supporting a high level of mixing, as the range of winter locations of birds from H.J. Andrews overlapped widely with birds from other breeding locations. Nevertheless, birds from Yosemite, the most southerly breeding site we sampled, wintered in the easternmost locations, Strong migratory connectivity could 'carry over' the effects of stressors from wintering grounds to breeding grounds. This pattern has been observed in Golden-winged Warbler (Vermivora chrysoptera),

Wood thrush (Hylocichla mustelina) and other species with declining populations showing strong migratory connectivity to wintering grounds that are losing habitat (Newton 2006, Inger et al. 2010, Taylor and Stutchbury 2016, Kramer et al. 2018). In our study, the lack of strong migratory connectivity supports the notion that local variation in population trends across the breeding range may be more influenced by breeding-ground habitat loss and climate change (Betts et al. 2018, Phalan et al. 2019) rather than stressors in particular locations on the wintering grounds. This information would help us to assess the relative contribution of stressors across the annual cycle, and how much of it can be buffered by metapopulation processes.

div.head: Migration phenology and schedule
div.p: Migrating at the right time to match the timing of resource availability is critical for individual survival and reproductive success of migratory birds (Renfrew et al. 2013, Zurell et al. 2018, Visser and Gienapp 2019b, Shipley et al. 2020). The phenology and duration of each migration stage recorded by individual tracking data in our study confirms anecdotal field observations on Hermit Warbler seasonal movements and annual cycle patterns (Pearson 2020). Across all birds, departure dates from breeding grounds and wintering grounds, and arrival date to the breeding range, were relatively less variable among individuals than timing of arrival at the wintering grounds. The timing of wintering ground departure in spring was positively related to spring arrival timing on the breeding grounds; earlier departing birds arrived earlier at the breeding grounds.

After breeding, the birds depart the breeding grounds in late June to mid-July. Considering that most birds arrive at the breeding grounds in early May this indicates a relatively short breeding season to find mates, build nests, lay eggs, incubate eggs, and rear chicks through the nestling and post-fledging phases. No double brooding has been reported in Hermit Warblers (Pearson 2020), and given the short window to breed, they may not have time to have a second brood, or possibly even have limited window for re-nest following failure. This limited breeding window raises the question of whether this species can show sufficient plasticity to adapt to shifts in timing of food resources resulting from rapid climate change (Visser 2008, Schmaljohann andBoth 2017). Extension of the breeding season into late summer may be limited for Hermit Warblers by drought and excessive heat from seasonal climate which is advancing due to climate change (Abatzoglou et al. 2014, Mote et al. 2018). Long-distance neotropical migrants like Hermit Warblers are known to be less capable of advancing spring arrival dates in accordance with warming spring temperatures on the breeding grounds (Furnas andMcGrann 2018, Lehikoinen et al. 2019). In a study in western Oregon, Hermit Warbler spring arrival date did not advance significantly in the past three decades, while some other species showed changes in arrival dates up to two weeks (Robinson et al. 2019).

Hermit Warblers may therefore be particularly vulnerable to a shorter duration in favorable climatic conditions during the breeding season. Finding ecological correlates of migration phenology, especially regional and local microclimate variation driven by topography, elevation, and vegetation type, would be an important next step in understanding how Hermit Warbler' breeding season and migration might be limited under contemporary climate change.

div.head: Migration routes, speed and post-breeding molt
div.p: From our tracking data, we recorded birds moving slowly during the early portion of fall migration, compared to spring or late fall migration. During the fall migration period, we found that most birds moved south of their breeding locations to montane regions, but remained within the species' known breeding range. Several field observations describe birds migrating to or through higher elevation areas in July and August in the Sierra Nevada and California Coast Range (Pearson 2020). Our continuous tracking data on several individuals indicates that most birds migrate outside their breeding territories to montane, higherelevation regions as they start their migration. The known molting period, after breeding, but before arriving at the wintering grounds (Jackson et al. 1992), and movements from our tracking study suggest that Hermit Warblers from Oregon and Washington migrate and presumably molt after leaving their breeding locations in montane regions of Northern California and Sierra Nevada. Knowledge of the exact location of stopover sites across this period is limited due to the precision of the location estimates using geolocators. However, the most likely locations during post-breeding show that they move with short hops between short stopovers, rather than staying for longer periods at a few distinguishable staging locations for molting (Figure 4.2 & Figure 4.3). Given that molting is energy intensive and reduces flight efficiency (Weimerskirch et al. 1995, Cantarero et al. 2014), habitat conditions on molting grounds can be critical for successful migration and survival. Habitat conditions at higher elevations during July-September could be a conservation concern as rapid climate change is introducing extreme heatwaves and drought that stresses plants, reduces ecosystem productivity and facilitates intense fires (Chmura et al. 2011, Sheehan et al. 2015).

During spring migration, Hermit Warblers moved quickly and did not show any evidence of extended periods of stay between wintering and breeding ranges (Figure 4.3). This short window of migration likely required much greater energetic expenditures than protracted fall migration, which would make molting during migration too energetically costly. Current literature reports pre-alternate molt of face, crown, throat and chin feathers occur in wintering grounds (Jackson et al. 1992), which also supports no molt migration during the spring migration, although it may not interfere with flight efficiency as no flight feathers are lost due to molt during this period. In addition, the rapid spring migration of male Hermit Warblers may be driven by sexual selection, wherein males compete for territories to be selected by females for breeding (Kokko 1999). Hermit Warblers' may have limited capability to adapt their migration phenology for breeding because of multiple factors. Their phenotypic plasticity for spring arrival may be limited by environmental cues for the onset of migration at the wintering range, while the climatic conditions and resource availability at the breeding grounds can reduce the fitness for early-arriving individuals. For instance, high elevation forests in Pacific Northwest could be still too cold for canopy arthropod activity when birds first arrive in the spring, which could reduce food availability. Together with previous studies showing limited flexibility in spring phenology in Hermit Warblers (Mayor et al. 2017a, Furnas and McGrann 2018, Robinson et al. 2019), our results on breeding duration and spring migration characteristics suggest that Hermit Warblers may have limited adaptive capacity to keep up with phenological matching of resources.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Conservation of this narrow-niched, climate-sensitive species under the current rate of climate change and habitat loss (Abatzoglou and Williams 2016, Berner et al. 2017, Phalan et al. 2019) will be challenging without a better understanding of its annual movement (Marra et al. 2015). Our study found diffuse migratory connectivity and subtle pattern of chain migration in Hermit Warblers, indicating that broad-scale changes on wintering grounds could be carried over to the breeding ranges, and a potentially high level of mixing between individuals across their range. However, an overlapping chain migration pattern suggests that southern breeding populations may be more tied to habitat and climatic changes on wintering grounds in southeastern Mexico. Phenology of migration was more similar across birds in spring, when birds migrated faster and directly toward breeding grounds than in fall, indicating that birds may be limited in their ability to adapt their spring phenology to match phenology of resources and thermal environment. Fall migration routes and speed suggest molt-migration to montane regions California for northern breeding birds, which may imply importance of conserving this key habitat for this species throughout its annual cycle. Finding ecological correlates of migration phenology, especially regional and local microclimate, topography, elevation, and vegetation in breeding and non-breeding ranges would be an important next step. div.head: Site
div.p: Hermit Warblers are a declining species in the H.J. Andrews and they benefited from cooler microclimates. I successfully tracked 22 adult male Hermit Warblers from across their breeding range. I found weak migratory connectivity, with a wide spatial overlap on the wintering grounds among birds from different breeding locations. Birds breeding in Yosemite National Park, the southernmost breeding location in our study, wintered farther east and south than birds from more northerly breeding locations. This provides some evidence for chain migration. I also found that they may use the montane regions in northern California and the Sierra Nevada for post-breeding molt, as they migrate slowly at this location after breeding during the molt period (Jackson et al., 1992).

In the last chapter, weak migratory connectivity in Hermit Warblers may imply that broad-scale climate change impacts on wintering grounds will affect populations on the breeding grounds. This provides important background that will enable modeling the full annual cycle population dynamics of this species of concern. Also, we found that Hermit Warblers have short breeding seasons and thus may be time-limited during their annual migratory cycle. This limitation can make them more prone to climate change-driven phenological mismatches in the breeding grounds.

Overall, my findings from South Korea and Oregon are consistent with the global trend in declines of common bird species. These declines in common land birds are likely to affect reductions in ecosystem services (e.g., control of arthropod populations, cultural services) they provide. Given our knowledge that long-term, large-scale bird population monitoring data are scarce in many regions, reassessments of population status and investments on surveillance monitoring on avian biodiversity is needed in most parts of the world. Major drivers in common bird declines were changes in land-cover and use and climate change as expected. Identifying important cover types and vegetation characteristics that can provide microclimate refugia could be an essential first step toward providing information for landuse planning and conservation planning to reduce avian biodiversity loss under climate warming. Birds from the H.J. Andrews Experimental Forest wintered across a broad geographic range in Mexico (Figure4.2). Although we observed overlap of wintering locations of birds from different breeding locations, in general the birds breeding in eastern longitudes wintered farther east (slope = 0.502, 90% CI= 0.035 -0.936) and south (slope =-0.518, 90% CI =-1.003 --0.032) than birds from higher latitudes and western longitudes(Table 4.2, Figure 4.4).

Most birds from Oregon and Washington moved south along the Cascades, to northern California's Sierra Nevada and Central Valley, then moved southeast toward Arizona and New Mexico to reach Mexico (Figure 4.2A-G). One bird from H.J. Andrews and another bird from Gifford Pinchot moved along the southern Coast Range in California, reaching near Los Angeles before moving southeast. Birds from Yosemite and Mendocino moved to southern California before moving southeast (Figure 4.2B & E). Birds arrived at their winter range (defined by longitude) from September to October, except for one bird from Gifford Pinchot that arrived in November. Upon leaving the breeding range, birds moved slowly in the early portion of their fall migration, then moved faster as they approached their wintering range (Figure 4.3). During spring migration (mean = 40.8 days, S.D. = 8.3 days), birds moved much faster than during fall migration (mean = 87.4 days, S.D = 20.2 days), moving north then diagonally northwest toward their breeding range in the Pacific coast states of the United States. Overall duration of migration was 46.5 days (95% CI = 38.242 -54.776), shorter on average during spring migration compared to fall migration (Figure 4.3. one-sample t-test, t = 11.700, p < 0.001). In fall, migration duration tended to be more variable than in spring (Figure 4.3).

Correlations between breeding versus wintering ground latitudes and longitudes suggest some form of chain migration, especially for individuals in the Sierra Nevada that may migrate farther south and east along the Central American landmass. BBS data suggest strong evidence of decline in Hermit Warblers breeding across their range, but the rate of decline is even stronger in the Sierra Nevada and Washington during 1993-2019(Sauer et al. 2020). While all of their breeding range is experiencing warming temperatures and forest loss from fires in recent years(Abatzoglou et al. 2014, Abatzoglou and Williams 2016), deforestation in southeastern states of Mexico, where birds from Yosemite and Washington wintered is most pronounced in the past decades(Aide et al. 2013, Bonilla-Moheno and Aide 2020). If birds breeding in Sierra Nevada and Washington use southeastern Mexico for wintering grounds, as our birds from Yosemite National Park suggest, they may be confronting increasing anthropogenic stressors in both the breeding and wintering stages of their annual cycle.Further studies using tracking devices or intrinsic markers such as stable isotopes of feathers molted in the winter range could focus on the breeding population in southern breeding range (e.g., southern Sierra Nevada, San Bernardino Mountains, southern California Coast Range) and Klamath Mountains to fill a knowledge gap in this area (seeFurnas et al. 2020 for detailed distribution of breeding population of Hermit Warblers in California). Although our study covers most of the Hermit Warbler breeding range, future studies should expand to these geographically and acoustically distinct breeding populations(Furnas et al. 2020) to capture the species' complete migration pattern and connectivity to the wintering grounds. For example, Hermit Warblers occur farther south in Central America from Guatemala to Costa Rica during winter months (NatureServe and BirdLife International 2014, eBird 2021), but none of our birds wintered farther south than southern Mexico.

Overall, we found that populations of six species declined over our eight-year study, in comparison to nine that exhibited increases, and five with no detectable trend (Figure 3.4). These local population trends are consistent with regional population trends in Oregon for Yellow-rumped Warbler, Wilson's Warbler, Golden-crowned Kinglet, andHermit Warblers, based on the Breeding Bird Survey (1993-2019;Sauer et al. 2020). Among the declining species, Hermit Warblers, Golden-crowned Kinglet and Chestnut-backed Chickadees are some of the most common songbird species in the watershed (31% of total individual detections in this study, combined). Considering their prevalence and their ecological function as secondary consumers, declines in these common taxa are potentially concerning for maintaining ecological functions as well as the ecological services (e.g., insect regulation) that they provide in forest ecosystems (Campbell et al. 1983, Harris et al. 2020).

Importantly, rates of bird population declines were not evenly distributed across the watershed. Among all examined species, models for eight species supported either one of our hypotheses (microclimate buffering and insurance hypotheses; Table 3.1, Figure 3.5). Population trends of these eight species were strongly negatively related to warmer microclimates (Figure 3.5AB), supporting the microclimate buffering hypothesis (Figure 3.1A). For these eight species, population trends were more negative in warmer locations, while negative population trends were dampened in cool microclimates (Figure 3.5). During the breeding season, below-canopy microclimates tend to be much cooler in oldgrowth forests (up to 2.5 o C; Frey et al. 2016), at higher elevations, and in locations with concave microtopographies (Frey et al. 2016, Rupp et al. 2020, Wolf et al. 2021). Consequently, our results support the idea that forests with complex structure and composition could buffer negative effects of warmingparticularly if they are located at high elevations and in complex terrain.

Current and projected future warming during the spring breeding period in the Pacific Northwest (Abatzoglou et al. 2014, Weiskopf et al. 2020, IPCC 2021) suggests that declining population trends for the four warming-sensitive species (Wilson's and Hermit Warblers, Golden-crowned Kinglet and Chestnut-backed Chickadees) may continue. Even species that appear stable (Red Crossbill) or increasing (Swainson's Thush, Pacific Wren, and Pacific-slope Flycatcher) may begin to decline as spring breeding season temperatures increase in the future, given the relationship between their population trends and microclimate temperatures observed in this study. Under rapid climate change, past clearcutting of oldgrowth forests in the Pacific Northwest (Strittholt et al. 2006, Krankina et al. 2014) and current intensive management of forests combine to limit the availability of microclimatic refugia needed to reduce the negative impacts of global warming on bird populations. div.head: Comparison of return rates between control and geolocator-tagged individuals
div.p: We sought to assess the effect of geolocators on return rates without the effects of potential bias from habitat differences or effort on recapture and re-sighting. To control for potential habitat differences and effort, we selected a subset of locations at H.J. Andrews (8 locations, but each are not necessarily independent), where we released both geolocator-tagged birds (N=19) and control birds (N=24) in 2019

for return rate analysis. At each capture location, observers listened for singing males and used audio lures of conspecific songs to read color-band combinations or capture birds to identify individual birds.

We made a total of 36 attempts of recapture/re-sighting and 672 minutes of observations and net operation time (from the start of playback broadcasting until the end of each attempt). At each attempt, we often detected and identified multiple individual birds with color band combinations or lack of markings. We ceased broadcasting after 10 minutes when we detected no Hermit Warblers, and moved to the next location. We used Fisher's exact test with the base R function "fisher.test" to compare proportions of returned individuals between control birds and geolocator-tagged birds.

div.head: Location estimation using light data
div.p: We estimated locations of birds using light-level archival geolocators. We followed the general process of geolocator data analysis suggested by Lisvoski et al. (2020). The geolocators recorded light intensity at 2-minute intervals. We first identified twilight events using the "preprocessLight" function and automatically filtered out outlier twilight time values to remove effect of shading and artificial lights on estimating twilight times (those that are greater than 15 minutes from the 4-day moving average) with the "twilightEdit" function in the "TwGeos" package (Wotherspoon et al. 2016). Then, we estimated locations between each twilight event (noon and midnight) by fitting a threshold-based model with "estelleMetropolis" function in the "SGAT" package. We fitted and tuned a series of movement models using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulations with a set of priors (probability of stay and migration speed distribution). This model uses raw location estimates, movement speed distribution, error estimations from the calibration process, and a spatial mask that excludes locations from what is clearly not habitat (e.g., oceans). We used a buffered range map to avoid unrealistic movements outside the range, especially northern occurrences during the winter. We buffered range maps to allow for potentially larger movements outside the known range (NatureServe and BirdLife International 2014), at scales of 300-km (breeding and migration period ranges), and 900-km (winter range). We used a wider buffer in winter to avoid limiting the movement of the model that covers all potential land area in Central America, Mexico, southern Texas and New Mexico. div.head: Chapter 5: General Conclusion
div.p: I have demonstrated three essential steps of research that are needed for science-based land bird conservation under anthropogenic stressors. Three essential procedures were: 1) a quantitative population status assessment and identification of broad-scale drivers, 2) a fine-scale analysis of drivers of population dynamics in breeding habitat, identifying biophysical drivers and their interaction effects on bird population trends, and 3) identification of wintering grounds, migratory connectivity and migration ecology of a habitat specialist songbird that is adversely affected by the warming climate on the breeding grounds.

In the second chapter, I have assessed a previously unknown population status of 52 common Korean breeding bird species, using a historical dataset. Between 1997Between -2005Between and 2013Between -2019, 38% , 38% of the analyzed species (20/52) exhibited declining occupancy trends across South Korea. Seven species declined 46-95% during this period. Black-capped Kingfisher (Halcyon pileatea) exhibited a steep rate of decline (95% decline) between the two periods. Among declining species, long-distance migrants (9/20) and common species (14/20) showed more rapid declines than other groups. Declines of five species were associated with climate change, and two species appeared to be affected by land-cover change. However, causes of population change in other species (46/52) remain unclear, but are most likely due to nonbreeding season stressors, sources of direct mortality, and fine-scale habitat loss not assessed in my analyses. A comparison of our data with regional and IUCN global red lists revealed that the current species status of fourteen among twenty declining species in Korea does not have a quantitative means of population assessment, including the Black-capped Kingfisher. These results suggest immediate reassessment of the species across the range and regional conservation action to save the species. Without an effort to collect robust information that supports conservation actions, the loss of land bird populations and their diversity could pass unnoticed.

In North America, a broad-scale, multi-species surveillance monitoring program, the North American Breeding Bird Survey, monitors population trends of common and widespread birds. These monitoring data were used in revealing declines in western forest birds (Rosenberg et al., 2019), and recent analyses have shown that changes in forest vegetation, climate change and their interaction are related to those changes in bird populations (Betts et al., 2018;Northrup et al., 2019;Phalan et al., 2019).
